entry.summary: On February 6, 2026, Heroku’s leadership, headed by Nitin T. Bhat, declared a major strategic shift. The platform is now officially going into a "Sustaining Engineering Model." Sustaining engineering, in corporate buzzword language, means one thing: Maintenance Mode. What’s Actually Changing? If you’re currently using Heroku to power your apps, relax... your site won’t go down anytime soon. But the product roadmap is effectively going into stasis: No New Features: That’s right, the entire focus is now stability, security, and "keeping the lights on." Existing Customers: So if you’re already a subscriber via a credit card or existing Enterprise contract, you’re good to go, nothing changes for you. It's common to see @lru_cache used for quick singletons in Python. As you might guess from the name — that's not the intended purpose of the function. But that doesn't necessarily mean this opportunistic "trick" is bad. But it also has important drawbacks, especially when instantiation is slow. This is for two key reasons. If instantiation is not instant, lazily creating your singleton can cause unnecessary delays. entry.title: Why building a reliable inline rich text editor is still surprisingly hard
entry.summary: Rich text editing on the web looks like a solved problem — until you try to build something that works reliably in real-world apps. On paper, browsers have had contenteditable for years. The illusion of “it just works” Simple demos usually work fine: Type text They: Double click words That’s where things start breaking. The hardest part isn’t UI — it’s selection Most of the complexity I’ve seen comes from selection handling: Different browsers return slightly different selection ranges. And once your toolbar shows the wrong state — users lose trust instantly. Bundle size vs correctness tradeoff Many editors solve this by adding layers of abstraction: Virtual document models Command pipelines Large plugin ecosystems This works — but often at the cost of: Huge bundle sizes Slower startup Harder embedding into existing apps Sometimes you don’t need a full document engine. What I started focusing on instead While experimenting with editors in real projects, I found myself caring more about: • Selection normalization across browsers Instead of building “more features”, I tried removing everything non-essential. What I learned Selection edge cases matter more than feature count Toolbar trust is more important than UI beauty Consistency across browsers beats clever architecture Inline editing UX is mostly about tiny details Curious about other experiences If you’ve worked with rich text editing in production: What was your biggest pain point? If you’re curious what my experiments turned into, you can check it here: https://scribejs.top/ But I’m more interested in hearing how others solved these problems.
